2272.text: In Ps.142.7 the infinitive construct 'give thanks to' following deliverance from prison matches the base gloss of thanksgiving for rescue; no divergence.

2296.text: H3034 in Ps.142.7 carries only M49; the verse's role-T3 words (H3318H 'Bring', H3803 'surround', H1580 'deal bountifully') are separate strongs -- 'Bring me out' is God's operation directed toward the psalmist, but not H3034's own tag.

2307.text: H3034 co-occurs with M47 (soul/self, 'me') and M12 (righteous). First pass: the psalmist's own selfhood (M47) is the site from which thanksgiving arises upon deliverance, while the righteous (M12) are the community that will gather around him -- thanksgiving here bridges personal rescue and communal righteousness.

3200.text: Across this pass's occurrences the core Hiphil imperative/perfect/participle sense 'give thanks/praise' recurs as the dominant pattern in liturgical contexts: Isa.12.1, 2Chr.30.22, 2Chr.7.6, 2Chr.20.21, 2Chr.31.2, Ezra.3.11, Neh.12.24, Ps.109.30, Isa.12.4, Jer.33.11, Ps.7.17, 1Chr.16.4, 1Chr.29.13, Ps.35.18, Ps.118.21, Ps.52.9, Ps.107.8/15/21/31, Ps.100.4, Ps.136.1/2/3/26, Ps.33.2, 2Chr.5.13, 1Chr.16.7, Neh.12.46, Ps.138.4, Ps.138.1, 2Chr.7.3, 1Chr.23.30, 1Chr.25.3, Ps.142.7, Neh.11.17 -- all render the same basic act of vocal, often corporate/musical, thanksgiving directed at the Lord, frequently anchored by the refrain 'his steadfast love endures forever.'

4943.text: In 2Chr.14.7 'we have sought the Lord our God... he has given us peace' extends the devotional sense (1a3a) into a covenant-causation frame -- seeking is presented as the ground of national security/peace, a nuance beyond the punctual consultation sense seen elsewhere and matching 2Chr.14.4's devotional register.

4961.text: In 2Chr.14.7, 'we' (Judah, T8/T11 party) is the initiator of the seeking, directed toward the Lord our God (T7 party) -- the operation is presented as the cause of the peace subsequently given, a covenant-causal relation between party and party.

4971.text: In 2Chr.14.7, M83 (sought) co-occurs with M02/M50 (still ours, H6440G, land/presence) and M33 (given us peace, H5117) and M46 (prospered, H6743B); here the seeking-of-the-Lord is presented as the causal ground for the peace and prosperity that follow, making M83 the operative characteristic upon which the other outcomes depend within this verse.

6171.text: In Luke.19.3 'was seeking to see who Jesus was' sits within the base gloss 'to seek, look for' -- an ordinary conative/intentional use (seeking-to-do-X), matching the well-attested infinitive-complement pattern.

6180.text: In Luke.19.3, M15 (seeing) co-occurs. Seeking here is the enabling desire behind the attempted act of seeing -- seeking-to-see names Zacchaeus's intent, while seeing (M15) names the not-yet-achieved perceptual goal; the two are linked as intent-and-object rather than independent themes.

7275.text: Across the verses both patterns occur: seeking/inquiring often precedes a resulting belief or outcome (e.g. 2Chr.14.7 'we have sought the Lord... he has given us peace', Ps.34.4 'I sought the Lord, and he answered me'), while elsewhere the failure or presence of seeking follows from an already-settled disposition (Ps.10.4's pride precedes and explains the non-seeking; 2Chr.12.14's evil is explained by not having set the heart to seek). The characteristic functions bidirectionally as both antecedent to and consequence of belief/judgement.

7276.text: Several occurrences orient the seeker toward a future promised fullness -- life (Amos.5.4,6,14 'Seek...and live'), finding/being found (Jer.29.13 'You will seek me and find me'), and restored peace/prosperity (2Chr.14.7) -- showing darash is not only a present act but a movement toward an anticipated covenantal reward not yet possessed.

7277.text: The immediate response to seeking is varied across contexts: it produces answer/deliverance (Ps.34.4), peace (2Chr.14.7), prospering (2Chr.26.5), being found (Jer.29.13), but also, when directed at illegitimate objects, provokes divine anger (2Chr.25.15) or judgment ('come to nothing', Amos.5.5). The response is consistently proportionate to the legitimacy of the object sought, not uniform in kind.

7278.text: Where the immediate response to seeking is a discrete event (an answer, a deliverance, a single oracle), the sustained effect is a settled state of peace, prosperity, or ongoing relationship: 2Chr.14.7 moves from the single act of seeking to years of peace and building; 2Chr.26.5 links sustained seeking ('as long as he sought the Lord') to sustained prospering, showing the sustained effect is durative and conditional on continued seeking rather than a one-time reward.

7321.text: Seeking produces peace and prosperity (2Chr.14.7 'we have sought the Lord... he has given us peace on every side'; 2Chr.26.5 'as long as he sought the Lord, God made him prosper') by the mechanism of covenantal blessing responsive to faithful devotion -- the mechanism is relational/covenantal reward rather than mechanical causation.

14522.text: Where it comes from. This is where the texts give most. The roots named in the context of these verses: Forgetting. "take care lest you forget the Lord" (Deu 6:12); "You were unmindful of the Rock that bore you, and you forgot the God who gave you birth" (Deu 32:18); Fullness. "Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked; you grew fat, stout, and sleek; then he forsook God who made him" (Deu 32:15); "when … they have eaten and are full and grown fat, they will turn to other gods" (Deu 31:20). Plenty comes before the turn; A deceived or turning heart. "Take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside" (Deu 11:16); "a man or woman … whose heart is turning away today" (Deu 29:18); Solomon's "heart had turned away" (1Ki 11:9), because "his wives turned away his heart" (1Ki 11:4); False security in the heart. The man who "blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart'" (Deu 29:19). Here the anger is said to refuse forgiveness to one man, singled out: "The Lord will not be willing to forgive him … the anger of the Lord and his jealousy will smoke against that man" (29:20); Intermarriage. "they would turn away your sons from following me" (Deu 7:4); Distress. "In the time of his distress he became yet more faithless to the Lord — this same King Ahaz. For he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him" (2Ch 28:22–23). Distress drives Ahaz further from God, not back. Contrast §16, where distress leads to crying out; Stubbornness, and not believing. "they would not listen, but were stubborn, as their fathers had been, who did not believe in the Lord their God" (2Ki 17:14); "I know how rebellious and stubborn you are" (Deu 31:27).

15036.text: The passage. Goliath challenges the ranks of Israel (17:8–10), and Saul and Israel are "dismayed and greatly afraid" (17:11). Every morning and evening for forty days (17:16) the same words, and "All the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him and were much afraid" (17:24). David hears (17:23), asks (17:26), is rebuked by Eliab (17:28; told in 10.15), tells Saul "Let no man's heart fail because of him" (17:32), and goes out "in the name of the Lord of hosts" (17:45).

15195.text: The boast is not removed. It is moved: The command. "Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord" (1Co 1:31; 2Co 10:17). This follows Christ "who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption" (1:30). It is joined to "it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends" (2Co 10:18); What to boast in; "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight" (Jer 9:24); The boast is in knowing God, and what is known is his character; The soul's boast. "My soul makes its boast in the Lord; let the humble hear and be glad" (Psa 34:2, carried); Not in my bow. "For not in my bow do I trust ... In God we have boasted continually" (Psa 44:6–8). The psalm then turns: "But you have rejected us" (44:9). The boast in God is kept in the psalm even while the defeat is brought before him; His name. "Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice!" (Psa 105:3; 1Ch 16:10); The worm. "Fear not, you worm Jacob ... you shall rejoice in the Lord; in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory" (Isa 41:14–16). The one called a worm is the one who glories; Justified and glorying. "Only in the Lord, it shall be said of me, are righteousness and strength ... In the Lord all the offspring of Israel shall be justified and shall glory" (Isa 45:24–25); The nations. If Israel returns and swears in truth, "nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory" (Jer 4:2); Exulting; "all who swear by him shall exult" (Psa 63:11); "Let the righteous one rejoice in the Lord and take refuge in him! Let all the upright in heart exult!" (Psa 64:10); "that I may glory with your inheritance" (Psa 106:5); The cross. "far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world" (Gal 6:14); Christ, not the flesh. "glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh — though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also" (Php 3:3–4). Paul has standing in the flesh, "I have more", and sets it aside; Hope, sufferings, God. ESV renders kauchaomai "rejoice" here:; "we rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings" (Rom 5:2–3); "we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation" (5:11); The same word that elsewhere is a proud boast is here joy in hope, in suffering, and in God; Held fast. "if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope" (Heb 3:6); The conscience. "our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God" (2Co 1:12). The boast is a clear conscience, and its ground is named as grace.

18878.text: Hiding from people: Much of the hiding in Scripture is from people who could do harm, and in these verses it is the weaker side that hides. "When the wicked rise, people hide themselves" (Proverbs 28:28). "The poor of the earth all hide themselves" (Job 24:4). When Israel hid in the caves, "all the people followed him trembling" (1 Samuel 13:7).; Often the verse records not the feeling of the one who hides but someone else's counsel to hide.; Jonathan: "Saul my father seeks to kill you … Stay in a secret place and hide yourself" (1 Samuel 19:2).; God to Elijah: "hide yourself by the brook Cherith" (1 Kings 17:3).; Where the feeling is named, it is fear.; Jacob fled from Laban "secretly", and he said why: "Because I was afraid" (Genesis 31:27, 31).; Joseph of Arimathea was "a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews". The same verse ends with him going to Pilate and taking away the body (John 19:38).; Hiding can be good sense: "The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it" (Proverbs 22:3). It ends when the news changes. The men who had hidden in the hills "heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they too followed hard after them in the battle" (1 Samuel 14:22).; And sometimes hiding is refused, or impossible.; The servant chooses not to hide: "I gave my back to those who strike … I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting" (Isaiah 50:6).; No one can hide from a friend who turns: "it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me — then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend" (Psalm 55:12–13).

18882.text: Hiding another: God hides people too, and those he hides ask for it.; "Hide me in the shadow of your wings" (Psalm 17:8).; "You hide them from the plots of men; you store them in your shelter from the strife of tongues" (Psalm 31:20).; The servant is hidden to be used later: "in the shadow of his hand he hid me; he made me a polished arrow; in his quiver he hid me away" (Isaiah 49:2).; At the last, a life is hidden in someone: "your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3).; There is a false shelter too: "we have made lies our refuge, and in falsehood we have taken shelter" (Isaiah 28:15).

18891.text: Who hides whom. God hiding a person is safety. God hiding his face from a person is dismay. The two are four verses apart in one psalm (Psalm 27:5, 9; 10.9).

19198.text: (f) Hiding as prudence. Pro 22:3 = 27:12, "The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it." The sequence is seeing leads to judging leads to hiding. The failure is the simple one's: seeing without acting.

19200.text: How it co-exists across the strands. Trembling (1Sa 13:7; Dan 10:7), fear (Gen 31:31; Joh 19:38), and seeing danger (Pro 22:3; 1Ch 21:20). Its opposite is the prudent/simple pair (f).

19201.text: Seat.; In the verse: 2Ch 22:9 "heart". The word has a genuine inner-being sense, but the heart is Jehoshaphat's, the dead grandfather's: "who sought the Lord with all his heart". Ahaziah, the one hiding, has no seat. Spurious for this phenomenon (v1 §0). Batch C v3 §7.1 read it as seeking the Lord with the heart. Batch G v3 §16.11 read it as "a dead man honoured for his grandfather's heart". Both readings stand. Neither concerns hiding.; Whose seat: none of the 40 hiders has one. In strand (a) the inner operation belongs to the counsellor, and it is shown by what the counsellor says, not by a seat word (v2, kept above).; Outside the verse — new in v3. In strand (a), the nearest seat word is *nephesh* in its life sense: the life being hunted. David, in the psalm headed by the Ziphites' report that he is "hiding among us" (Psa 54:1), says "the Lord is the upholder of my life" (54:4). The seat word names what is at stake in the hiding, not where the hider feels it. This fits Batch G v3 §5 ("Life spared, life hunted — the *nephesh* as a prize"), which it does not change.; Strand (f), prudence — new in v3: Pro 22:3 ("The prudent sees danger and hides himself") → 22:5 "Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them". The prudent one's hiding is a guarding of the soul. *Nephesh* here is the self that is kept from harm, and it passes the check in that sense. Strand (f) is the only strand of §2 where the one who hides has a seat, and the seat is the thing the hiding protects.

19205.text: Where it comes from. A threat to life. Notably, in three verses the threat is speech: "the strife of tongues" (Psa 31:20), "the lash of the tongue" (Job 5:21), "secret plots" (Psa 64:2).

The same verb gives safety (§3) and dread (§5), depending on whether God hides the person or hides himself from the person. v3 adds that the heart between them, "My heart says to you, 'Your face, Lord, do I seek'" (27:8), is seeking the face.
